questions.question: India's flexible inflation-targeting framework, adopted via a 2016 RBI Act amendment, targets:
options: CPI inflation of 4% with a 2–6% band
WPI inflation of 2%
GDP growth of 8%
Money supply growth of 15%
questions.rationale: The amended RBI Act (Section 45ZA) fixes the target as 4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of two percentage points on either side.

questions.question: The Monetary Policy Committee consists of:
options: Three members, all from the RBI
Nine members drawn from banks
Six members — three from the RBI and three government nominees
Only the Finance Minister and the RBI Governor
questions.rationale: The MPC has six members: the RBI Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor for monetary policy, one RBI officer, and three government-nominated experts, deciding by majority vote.

questions.question: The repo rate is the rate at which:
options: Banks lend to their best customers
The RBI lends short-term to banks against securities
The RBI borrows from the government
Banks lend to each other overnight
questions.rationale: Repo is the RBI's short-term collateralised lending rate to banks — the main policy lever that sets the cost of credit in the economy.

questions.question: If the RBI raises the CRR, the immediate effect is that:
options: Banks have more funds to lend
The rupee automatically depreciates
Government borrowing becomes cheaper
The credit multiplier shrinks and lendable deposits fall
questions.rationale: A higher CRR locks more deposits as cash with the RBI, lowering the money multiplier (1/CRR) and contracting credit — a tightening move.

questions.question: Under open market operations, the RBI fights inflation by:
options: Selling government securities to banks
Buying government securities from banks
Printing new currency notes
Raising the SLR to 100%
questions.rationale: Selling securities absorbs money from the banking system; buying injects liquidity — so sales are the tight-money, anti-inflation move.

questions.question: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), introduced in 2022, is notable because it:
options: Lends to banks without collateral
Replaces the repo rate as the main policy rate
Absorbs banks' surplus funds without needing collateral
Applies only to foreign banks
questions.rationale: The SDF absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral, replacing the fixed-rate reverse repo as the liquidity corridor's floor.

questions.question: Raising the margin requirement on loans against sensitive commodities is an example of:
options: A quantitative tool
A qualitative (selective) tool of monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Debt management
questions.rationale: Margin requirements, selective credit controls, credit rationing, and moral suasion are qualitative instruments aimed at particular markets.

questions.question: Moral suasion as a monetary tool means the RBI:
options: Legally compels banks to cut lending
Persuades banks through meetings, letters, and public statements
Fines banks for excess credit
Nationalises erring banks
questions.rationale: Moral suasion is informal pressure — guidance without formal orders — a classic qualitative instrument.

questions.question: In the transmission mechanism, a repo rate increase first affects:
options: Retail prices directly
Banks' cost of funds, which passes into lending rates
The government's tax collections
The exchange rate only
questions.rationale: The chain runs: repo rises → banks' funding cost rises → lending rates reset → credit and demand cool → inflation eases, over several quarters.

questions.question: Which combination represents an easy money policy?
options: Lower repo rate and purchase of securities
Higher CRR and sale of securities
Higher repo rate with higher margin requirements
Higher bank rate with credit rationing
questions.rationale: Easy (cheap) money cuts rates, lowers reserve ratios, and buys securities to expand credit — used against recession, not inflation.
